rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic — water-resources governance study unrelated to household or community service access, per Exclusion Criterion 7; also fails Criterion 2 narrow rule-type scope and Criterion 4 service-access outcome). title: The perception of users about the impacts of water rationing on their household routines
rationale: Excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure) under the 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism clarification to Criterion 2. title: Thirst for what? Effects of political interference in the sanitation sector on the welfare and expansion of the system; [SEDE DE QUÊ? EFEITOS DA INTERFERÊNCIA POLÍTICA NO SETOR DE SANEAMENTO SOBRE O BEM-ESTAR E A EXPANSÃO DO SISTEMA]
rationale: Excluded primarily under E04 (Wrong outcome), and also failing the narrow 2026-10-13 reading of Criterion 2. Although the title refers to effects of political interference in the sanitation sector on welfare and expansion of the system, full-text review shows that system expansion (n2) and welfare are modeled exclusively in a stylized two-period microeconomic theoretical model (Section 3) with no empirical testing. In the empirical panel-data econometric analysis (Section 4, Tables 2-3, N = 983 municipality-year observations, 2002-2021), the sole dependent variable is Variação_real, the annual real percentage tariff adjustment authorized by subnational regulatory agencies (nominal adjustment minus IPCA), while municipal water and sewage coverage rates (atend_agua, atend_esgoto) enter only as right-hand-side explanatory variables. Thus, no empirical household or community service access, connection, availability, continuity, quantity, household affordability, or exclusion outcome is reported (c4 = no). Additionally, under the narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 scope, the empirical exposure tested is municipal and state election years (macro-political electoral cycles) rather than a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing service access (c2 = no; under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the study passes c2 as a regulatory/governance study of political interference in regulatory agencies, but plain_criterion2_decision remains 'exclude' due to failing Criterion 4).

Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it would be included because it discusses metropolitan institutional governance, municipal delegation to state utility CEDAE, historical state reorganization, and bulk-supply contracting. Under the active rule-type scope, however, its empirical explanatory focus is the physical/socio-technical path-dependence of centralized macro-infrastructure (trunk pipeline capacities, missing storage reservoirs, and core-biased capital engineering plans) with institutional history serving only as macro-governance background rather than analyzing a legal, regulatory, or administrative rule governing household access.

It satisfies all eligibility criteria (c1-c6): under both the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type clarification, formal utility ownership/delegation and regulatory contracting structures (consortia vs. standalone municipal provision) directly analysed against population water and sanitation service coverage are eligible, though confidence is rated medium because the institutional mechanism operates at the municipal utility-governance and contracting level rather than household-level administrative rules.

title: What Determines Access to Piped Water in Rural Areas? Evidence from Small-Scale Supply Systems in Rural Brazil
rationale: Barde (2017) empirically evaluates how the institutional ownership and management structure of rural piped-water service providers affects rural household connection rates across Brazilian municipalities between 2000 and 2010. Both treatment and control municipalities established new small-scale rural water supply systems during 2000-2008, isolating the provider/ownership regime (autonomous or concession-holding community water user associations vs. municipal governments/public firms, alongside regional state-owned utilities vs. municipal utilities) rather than merely comparing infrastructure presence vs. absence. Although framed partly in terms of participatory vs. non-participatory project choice and local electoral/media accountability, its core exposure directly examines utility/provider ownership and governance structure governing water service access, satisfying all inclusion criteria (c1-c6) under both the plain wording and the 2026-10-13 narrow reading of Criterion 2.

title: The impact of household connection to public network wastewater systems: Regulatory impact assessment
rationale: Excluded (primary code E03; also fails on c4/c5 and prospective non-evaluative study design E12). Although the paper addresses the household connection gap to public wastewater networks in four Brazilian municipalities regulated by ARSAE (c1 = yes) and mentions mandatory connection statutes (Law no. 11445/2007, art. 45; Law no. 13317/1999, art. 48) and tariff incentives as institutional background, it does not examine a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism governing service access under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 scope. Instead, it demonstrates an ex-ante Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA) / Multiple Criteria Decision Analysis (M-MACBETH) exercise comparing four hypothetical infrastructure-diffusion targets (100%, 75%, 50%, and 0% reductions in non-connected households). Moreover, even under the plain wording of Criterion 2 (where RIA as a regulatory governance tool would pass c2), the paper is excluded because RIA was not implemented in practice, household connection levels (0; 26,768; 53,537; and 107,074 non-connected households) are exogenously assumed scenario inputs rather than empirically measured access outcomes, and the primary data consist solely of stakeholder preference weights used to rank hypothetical targets and their projected health, revenue, and sludge impacts.

title: Isomorphic mimicry and the effectiveness of water-sector reforms in Brazil
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). While the paper discusses water and sanitation service access in Brazil and examines legal, institutional, and regulatory structures (including Law no. 11.445/2007, Law no. 14.026/2020, decentralized subnational regulators, and the exclusion of rural and informal peri-urban areas from regulation), it is a narrative policy/institutional overview and conceptual essay arguing that reforms suffer from isomorphic mimicry. It presents no empirical research design, no primary qualitative or quantitative data, no empirical analysis of secondary micro/panel data, and no systematic review methodology.

title: After the summit: women's access to water and policymaking in Brazil
rationale: Excluded as E05 (No empirical evidence). Leite (2010) is a narrative policy and advocacy essay in Gender & Development arguing for gender mainstreaming and women's participation in Brazilian water policymaking after the 1992 Earth Summit. It reports no primary empirical data, no empirical methodology or study design, and is not a systematic empirical synthesis; its two brief community case studies (São João D'Aliança and Santa Cruz da Baixa Verde) are purely secondary summaries cited to GWA web pages and conference papers (GWA 2006a; Almeida and Chalub-Martins 2008; Branco and Almeida 2002). In addition, under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type clarification of Criterion 2, the paper fails Criterion 2 because it focuses on macro-governance commitments and NGO-supported environmental education, riverbank restoration, and leadership promotion rather than a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing service access. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study remains excluded due to the absence of empirical evidence (E05).

title: Basic Sanitation in Brazil: Lessons from the Past, Opportunities from the Present, Challenges for the Future
rationale: Full-text review of Heller (2007) confirms that although the article addresses water supply and sanitation access in Brazil (c1) and discusses institutional, concession, cost-recovery, and statutory frameworks including PLANASA and Law No. 11,445 of 2007 (c2), it is a non-empirical historical and public-policy overview essay. It presents no empirical study design, no primary qualitative or quantitative data, and no systematic empirical synthesis, relying solely on descriptive secondary statistics and policy commentary while noting that deeper methodological and case-study work is ongoing elsewhere. It is therefore excluded as E05 (No empirical evidence) under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2.

title: Expert group decision-making on ESG strategies for water public sanitation utilities under fiscal and budgetary constraints in Brazil
rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic; also fails c2 under the narrow rule-type scope and c4 on outcome). The paper uses an adapted Nominal Group Technique survey (N = 54) in Maceio, Brazil to rank 34 candidate Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) strategies for advancing organizational ESG maturity in a state-owned utility under fiscal constraints. It does not examine household or community water/sanitation service access (c1 = no), does not empirically test a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism governing access (c2 = no; items like progressive social tariffs are only hypothetical strategies rated by respondents), and reports only Likert-scale strategy priority scores rather than any actual access, connection, reliability, affordability, or exclusion outcome (c4 = no). Even under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the study remains excluded because it fails Criteria 1 and 4.

title: (Des) governança da água e desastre: um estudo de caso sobre o rompimento da barragem da Lagoa da Conceição em Florianópolis
rationale: Exclude (E01: Wrong topic). Although the provided PDF text is truncated at page 74 of 291, it includes the complete Portuguese and English abstracts, full table of contents, complete lists of all 53 figures and 12 tables, Chapter 1 (problem statement, research question, general and specific objectives, and chapter-by-chapter summary), Chapter 2, and the opening of Chapter 3, which conclusively establish the study's scope. This 2024 Master's dissertation is a qualitative pragmatic case study of environmental/disaster water governance following the January 2021 rupture of an evapo-infiltration lagoon dam at CASAN's wastewater treatment plant in Lagoa da Conceição, Florianópolis. It examines public-arena actor networks, media vocabularies, ecological contamination of a coastal lagoon, flood damage to nearby residences, and post-disaster reparation controversies rather than household or community water or sanitation service access (failing c1 and c4) or any rule-type legal/administrative mechanism governing service access (failing narrow c2). Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the study would also be excluded because Criteria 1 and 4 are not satisfied.

title: Implementing Indigenous and Western Knowledge Systems in Water Research and Management (Part 1): A Systematic Realist Review to Inform Water Policy and Governance in Canada
rationale: Exclude under E01 (Wrong topic). This systematic realist review synthesizes 63 Canadian peer-reviewed and grey-literature documents on how Indigenous and Western knowledge systems and methodologies are integrated in water research and broad environmental/resource management (e.g., sea ice, watersheds, marine planning, and water quality/health research). Although drinking-water disparities are noted as background and broad water governance/co-management themes are catalogued (which would satisfy the plain wording of Criterion 2, though not the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism scope), the review does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access (c1=no), does not evaluate a rule-type legal/administrative mechanism governing service access (c2=no), and reports only bibliometric/epistemological research-practice findings rather than any service-access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcomes (c4=no).

title: Insights and Opportunities: Challenges of Canadian First Nations Drinking Water Operators
rationale: Excluded (E04 - Wrong outcome; also fails C1 and narrow C2). This primary mixed-methods empirical study interviews 8 Ontario First Nations water system operators and surveys 79 British Columbia First Nations water system operators regarding operator certification, working hours, wages, paid vacation, job satisfaction, workplace challenges, and operator retention. Although the paper discusses institutional and governance issues (operator certification, band council control over O&M budgets and hiring, and AANDC's 80:20 O&M funding formula including household/business user fees in 3 Ontario communities), these are examined only in relation to operator employment conditions and plant O&M resourcing rather than as rule-type mechanisms directly governing household or community water access (failing narrow C2), and the study reports only operator HR/workforce outcomes with no empirical measure of household or community water access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion (failing C1 and C4 under both plain and narrow readings of C2).

title: Square Peg, Round Hole: First Nations Drinking Water Infrastructure and Federal Policies, Programs, and Processes
rationale: This empirical qualitative grounded-theory study (13 interviews with 16 First Nations drinking water technical practitioners in Ontario, triangulated with 8 case studies) examines how federal administrative, fiscal, and institutional rules under the Indian Act and Treasury Board Project Approval Policy govern First Nations community drinking water infrastructure and service provision. It satisfies Criterion 2 under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism scope because it specifically analyzes multi-stage approval and reporting burdens (PPA/EPA, Level of Service Standards), the 20% local O&M cost-recovery/user-fee rule, March 31 fiscal-year expenditure rules, and rigid non-discretionary standardized procedures failing to accommodate remote and low-capacity bands, linking these mechanisms to delayed/piecemeal community water infrastructure availability, exclusion of remote communities from infrastructure development opportunities, and two-tier service delivery. Per review safeguards, qualitative socio-legal/policy studies with mechanism-relevant access/availability outcomes are included for the mechanism synthesis.

title: Multi-barrier protection of drinking water systems in Ontario: A comparison of First Nation and non-First Nation communities
rationale: Full text matches record R70B810197AA2 (Walters et al., 2012). The study empirically compares 143 First Nation community drinking water systems in Ontario (using 2005/2007 federal AANDC Risk Level Evaluation data obtained via Access to Information Act) against 54 non-First Nation municipal/township systems surveyed with the same instrument. It satisfies C1 and C4 at the community/utility level because, alongside water-quality safety, the risk evaluation and reported findings examine community drinking water service standards, treatment capacity to meet demand, operational reliability, occasional water shortages, and whether systems supply a sufficient volume of water to the community. It satisfies C2 under both the plain wording and (as a borderline community/system-level case) the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading by comparing utilities operating under two distinct regulatory, financing/cost-recovery, and enforcement structures in Ontario: municipal systems under binding provincial statutes and fee/tax cost recovery versus First Nation systems governed by non-statutory federal protocols, AANDC service-standard funding formulas, conditional 80/20 O&M cost-sharing, funding-withholding enforcement, and by-law opt-in conditions for provincial source water protection. Confidence is medium because the empirical analysis compares the two regimes at the aggregate First Nation vs. municipal group level and centers primarily on a multi-barrier drinking-water risk index rather than household-level access connections.

title: Boiling over: A Descriptive Analysis of Drinking Water Advisories in First Nations Communities in Ontario, Canada
rationale: Excluded under E03 (wrong exposure). Although this quantitative study examines an access/reliability proxy outcome (402 drinking water advisories and their duration in First Nations community water systems in Ontario from 2004 to 2013), its empirical analysis investigates only temporal/seasonal patterns (year, month, season via Poisson regression), technical failure causes (equipment malfunction, disinfection residuals, turbidity), and physical/operational system characteristics (water source, system age, population size, and primary operator technical training). Water governance issues—such as federal-provincial jurisdictional gaps, multi-agency fragmentation, and the Safe Drinking Water for First Nations Act—are discussed solely as unanalysed macro-governance background in the Discussion section rather than empirically examined, failing Criterion 2 under both the 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism scope and plain wording.

title: Indigenous peoples and water governance in Canada: Regulatory injustice and prospects for reform
rationale: Excluded as E05 (no empirical evidence; also out of scope on service access and outcome). This 2018 book chapter presents a narrative socio-legal, historical, and normative policy overview of Indigenous freshwater governance in British Columbia through two illustrative discussions drawn from secondary historical/legal literature and the authors' prior thesis and policy reports (Simms 2014; Joe et al. 2016/2017; Jollymore et al. 2017), without reporting any empirical study design, data-collection methods, or analytical procedures. Substantively, it also examines provincial surface-water resource allocation licensing (FITFIR) and legislative consultation on the BC Water Sustainability Act rather than household or community drinking-water or sanitation service access (c1=no, c2 narrow=no despite passing plain c2, c4=no, c5=no), so the decision is exclude under both the narrow and plain readings of Criterion 2.

title: Water (in)security in Canada: national identity and the exclusion of Indigenous peoples
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Although the article addresses Indigenous household and community water/wastewater access disparities in Canada, it is a conceptual and narrative essay arguing that settler-colonial national identity and neo-liberalism sustain Indigenous water insecurity. It reports no primary empirical data, no empirical research methods, and no systematic synthesis protocol; its 'five short case studies' are one-paragraph vignettes summarizing previously published papers and a newspaper report. Additionally, under the 2026-10-13 narrow reading of Criterion 2, its central focus is macro-governance/ideological background rather than empirical analysis of a specific rule-type access mechanism. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper remains excluded due to the absence of empirical evidence (E05).

title: Constructing community health and safety
rationale: This 10-year qualitative anthropological case study empirically examines household and community access to a municipal drinking-water watermain extension in Central Saanich, Canada, satisfying all inclusion criteria (c1-c6) under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Specifically, it documents how municipal waterline-extension and rural-zoning policies (RE-3 zoning and land-use bylaws), petition voting/land-value thresholds (50% of properties representing two-thirds of land value) and cost-recovery rules for extensions, municipal engineer discretion under Bylaw No. 1410, and municipal-versus-regional jurisdiction directly governed 30 years of household exclusion from piped municipal water and eventual approval. Qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are explicitly eligible for the systematic review's mechanism synthesis.

title: Water and Indigenous Peoples: Canada's Paradox
rationale: Excluded under E05 (no empirical evidence with identifiable data/methods; narrative policy overview and conceptual essay, not an empirical study or systematic synthesis). While the article examines safe drinking water and wastewater challenges on First Nations reserves in Canada (c1=yes) and discusses regulatory gaps, annual contribution agreements, 80/20 O&M cost-sharing rules, and proposed federal legislation (c2=yes at topic level under both plain and narrow readings), it has no methods section, no identifiable empirical study design, and no reported sample size, site selection, data collection, or analytic procedure for the brief illustrative focus-group quotes inserted on pages 10-11, nor does it empirically analyze a governance exposure against a primary service-access outcome (c3=no, c5=no).

title: Resisting Neo-Liberalism: The Poisoned Water Disaster in Walkerton, Ontario
rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic; also fails Criterion 4 on access outcomes and narrow Criterion 2). Snider (2004) presents a qualitative socio-legal case study of the May 2000 E. coli drinking-water contamination disaster in Walkerton, Ontario, and analyzes how discourses of law, science, and Canadian nationalism in the Walkerton Public Inquiry (O'Connor Report) challenged neo-liberal deregulation. While the paper examines regulatory and governance factors under the plain wording of Criterion 2 (laboratory privatization, non-binding reporting guidelines, MoE budget/inspection cuts, and non-enforcement), those rules govern drinking-water quality/safety rather than household or community service access, and the paper reports health/contamination and discursive/legislative outcomes rather than water or sanitation service access outcomes. Therefore, it is excluded under both the narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 reading and the plain Criterion 2 wording.

title: Water, sanitation and hygiene and indigenous peoples: a review of the literature
rationale: Excluded as E05 (no primary empirical evidence and not a systematic empirical synthesis of governance-to-access evidence). Jiménez, Cortobius, and Kjellén (2014) conduct a broad scoping/thematic literature review of 185 Scopus articles on indigenous peoples and water, grouping papers into six topic counts (Table 1) and providing a narrative overview without study-level data extraction, quality assessment, or empirical synthesis of exposures and service-access outcomes (failing Criteria 3, 4, and 5, so plain_criterion2_decision is also 'exclude'). Furthermore, under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2, its legal and institutional discussion focuses on natural-resource and river-basin water rights and co-management, behavioural hygiene promotion ('shared responsibility agreements'), general intercultural project delivery, and a brief two-sentence mention of cultural resistance to paying for water, rather than analyzing a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism governing household or community water or sanitation service access.

title: Multiple Disconnections: Environmental Justice and Urban Water in Canada and South Africa
rationale: Exclude under E05 (No empirical evidence). Although the article discusses urban water access and rule-type tariff, cost-recovery, credit-control, and utility-governance mechanisms in Hermanus (South Africa) and Toronto (Canada)—satisfying Criterion 1 and both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2—it is a theoretical political ecology essay problematising the multiscalar concept of environmental justice, illustrated with two brief narrative policy overviews. It has no methods or data section, no identifiable empirical study design or sample, and presents no primary empirical access outcome data (nor is it a systematic empirical synthesis), relying instead on secondary reports (such as DWAF, 1997b, and Deedat, Pape and Qotole, 2001) for Hermanus water demand and disconnection figures and newspaper/union accounts for the defeated 2002 Toronto governance proposal.

title: "We don't drink the water here": The reproduction of undrinkablewater for first Nations in Canada
rationale: Excluded under E03 (wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism clarification of Criterion 2. Although the paper examines First Nation household water cistern delivery and sanitation (c1=yes, c4=yes) and reports primary data from participatory source water protection risk-ranking exercises across six Prairie First Nation communities (c3=yes), its empirical analysis focuses on ranking physical contamination threats to source water (cracked cisterns, septic shoot-outs, open landfills). Colonial legal and institutional structures (the Indian Act 1876, Numbered Treaties, federal-provincial jurisdictional division, and exclusion from decision-making) provide macro-governance political-ecology framing rather than an empirically studied rule-type mechanism directly governing service access. Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the study would be included.

title: Reclaiming indigenous planning as a pathway to local water security
rationale: Exclude (E01: Wrong topic; also fails c2 narrow rule-type exposure and c4 access outcome). While the introduction discusses First Nations water infrastructure and colonial/constitutional water governance as background, the empirical study is a community-based participatory source water protection planning case study focused on identifying drinking-water contamination threats and initiating physical contamination-prevention actions (cistern cleaning, wellhead protection, well decommissioning, site remediation) alongside cultural empowerment. It does not examine water or sanitation service access (c1=no), does not evaluate a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism governing access under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 scope (c2=no; participatory contamination planning passes plain c2 wording as governance, but fails narrow rule-type scope), and reports no service-access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcomes (c4=no; hence plain_criterion2_decision is also exclude).

title: Wastewater management by citizens: mismatch between legal rules and self-organisation in Oosterwold
rationale: This qualitative socio-legal empirical case study satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. It investigates how statutory sewer mandates and waiver rules (Dutch Environmental Management Act s. 10.33), Crisis and Recovery Act experimental rules, anterior residency agreements, water board discharge permits, pollution levies, and ownership/provision structures directly governed household wastewater service provision and sewer connection in Oosterwold, Almere. Using doctrinal analysis, municipal/contractual document analysis, 19 semi-structured interviews, and water board monitoring data on 199 household onsite sewage facilities (OSSFs), it documents household reliance on individual OSSFs in the absence of public sewers, high OSSF operational failure/non-compliance (33 of 199 failing standards), and the resulting decision to connect non-compliant and future households to the public sewer network. Per review safeguards, qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are fully eligible for systematic review inclusion.

title: Consumer-inclusive economic regulation: water pricing under different regulatory regimes
rationale: Excluded (E04: Wrong outcome). Although this is an empirical comparative case study of three water pricing regulatory regimes (Vitens in The Netherlands, Agbar in Spain, and Scottish Water/WICS in Scotland), its sole analyzed outcome is procedural consumer inclusiveness in tariff-setting governance (transparency, consultation/participation, and administrative/parliamentary accountability in Table 3). It does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access (c1=no), does not evaluate an access, connection, reliability, disconnection, or affordability outcome (c4=no; descriptive coverage and annual household water bill figures in Table 2 are background case-selection context), and under the 2026-10-13 narrow reading of Criterion 2 analyzes procedural stakeholder participation rules rather than rule-type mechanisms directly governing service access (c2=no under narrow reading, yes under plain wording; excluded under both).

title: Peri-urban water and sanitation services: Policy, planning and method
rationale: Excluded under E05 (no empirical evidence). Record R975C44396921 (Kurian & McCarney, eds., 2010, DOI 10.1007/978-90-481-9425-4) is an entire 13-chapter edited pedagogical volume developed for a UNESCO-IHE distance-learning course on peri-urban water and sanitation policy, planning, and assessment methods. Although Chapters 1 and 2 conceptually discuss peri-urban water and sanitation service access (c1=yes) and rule-type mechanisms including connection tariffs/lifeline rates and tenure/legality barriers barring informal settlements from formal connections (c2=yes under both plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings), the volume as a whole is neither a primary empirical study of water/sanitation service access nor a systematic empirical synthesis (c3=no), and lacks a unified empirical study design, sample, exposure, and measured access outcome (c4=no, c5=no). Confidence is set to medium because PDF pages 75-326 of 326 were truncated by the input byte limit, though the complete front matter (Table of Contents, Lists of Boxes/Figures/Tables), complete Chapter 1 (including Section 1.5's summary of all chapters), and Chapter 2 pp. 27-42 (explicitly noting synthesis of prior reports Allen et al. 2006, 2007, 2008) establish the pedagogical overview nature of the book.
